---
title: cacheTag
description: Learn how to use the cacheTag function to manage cache invalidation in your Next.js application.
related:
  title: Related
  description: View related API references.
  links:
    - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents
    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache
    - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag
    - app/api-reference/functions/updateTag
    - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife
---

The `cacheTag` function allows you to tag cached data for on-demand invalidation. By associating tags with cache entries, you can selectively purge or revalidate specific cache entries without affecting other cached data.

## Usage

To use `cacheTag`, enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file:

```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig
```

```js filename="next.config.js" switcher
const nextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig
```

The `cacheTag` function takes one or more string values.

```tsx filename="app/data.ts" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getData() {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('my-data')
  const data = await fetch('/api/data')
  return data
}
```

```jsx filename="app/data.js" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getData() {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('my-data')
  const data = await fetch('/api/data')
  return data
}
```

You can then purge the cache on-demand from a [Server Function](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route):

- Use [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) for read-your-own-writes scenarios, such as forms and other user-triggered mutations, where a user makes a change and the next read should fetch fresh data immediately. `updateTag` is only available inside Server Functions.
- Use [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) when it is acceptable to serve stale data while revalidation happens in the background, or when revalidating from a [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) or other context.

For example, this Server Function adds a post and then purges every cache entry tagged `'my-data'` so the next read reflects the change:

```tsx filename="app/action.ts" switcher
'use server'

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'

export default async function submit() {
  await addPost()
  updateTag('my-data')
}
```

```jsx filename="app/action.js" switcher
'use server'

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'

export default async function submit() {
  await addPost()
  updateTag('my-data')
}
```

## Good to know

- **Idempotent Tags**: Applying the same tag multiple times has no additional effect.
- **Multiple Tags**: You can assign multiple tags to a single cache entry by passing multiple string values to `cacheTag`.

```tsx
cacheTag('tag-one', 'tag-two')
```

- **Limits**: A single `cacheTag()` call accepts up to 128 tags, each with a maximum length of 256 characters. Tags longer than 256 characters are skipped, and any tags past the 128th in one call are dropped. Both cases log a console warning.

## Examples

### Tagging components or functions

Tag your cached data by calling `cacheTag` within a cached function or component:

```tsx filename="app/components/bookings.tsx" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

interface BookingsProps {
  type: string
}

export async function Bookings({ type = 'haircut' }: BookingsProps) {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('bookings-data')

  async function getBookingsData() {
    const data = await fetch(`/api/bookings?type=${encodeURIComponent(type)}`)
    return data
  }

  return //...
}
```

```jsx filename="app/components/bookings.js" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function Bookings({ type = 'haircut' }) {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('bookings-data')

  async function getBookingsData() {
    const data = await fetch(`/api/bookings?type=${encodeURIComponent(type)}`)
    return data
  }

  return //...
}
```

### Creating tags from external data

You can use the data returned from an async function to tag the cache entry.

```tsx filename="app/components/bookings.tsx" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

interface BookingsProps {
  type: string
}

export async function Bookings({ type = 'haircut' }: BookingsProps) {
  async function getBookingsData() {
    'use cache'
    const data = await fetch(`/api/bookings?type=${encodeURIComponent(type)}`)
    cacheTag('bookings-data', data.id)
    return data
  }
  return //...
}
```

```jsx filename="app/components/bookings.js" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function Bookings({ type = 'haircut' }) {
  async function getBookingsData() {
    'use cache'
    const data = await fetch(`/api/bookings?type=${encodeURIComponent(type)}`)
    cacheTag('bookings-data', data.id)
    return data
  }
  return //...
}
```

### Invalidating tagged cache

Using [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag), you can invalidate the cache for a specific tag when needed:

```tsx filename="app/actions.ts" switcher
'use server'

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateBookings() {
  await updateBookingData()
  revalidateTag('bookings-data', 'max')
}
```

```jsx filename="app/actions.js" switcher
'use server'

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateBookings() {
  await updateBookingData()
  revalidateTag('bookings-data', 'max')
}
```

1 --- 2 title: cacheLife 3 description: Learn how to use the cacheLife function to set the cache expiration time for a cached function or component. 4 related: 5 title: Related 6 description: View related API references. 7 links: 8 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents 9 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache 10 - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag 11 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag 12 --- 13 14 The `cacheLife` function is used to set the cache lifetime of a function or component. It should be used alongside the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive, and within the scope of the function or component. 15 16 ## Usage 17 18 ### Basic setup 19 20 To use `cacheLife`, first enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file: 21 22 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 23 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 24 25 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 26 cacheComponents: true, 27 } 28 29 export default nextConfig 30 ``` 31 32 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 33 const nextConfig = { 34 cacheComponents: true, 35 } 36 37 export default nextConfig 38 ``` 39 40 `cacheLife` can only be used within a cache directive scope. 41 42 Add a cache directive (for example, `use cache`) at the file level or at the top of an async function or component. 43 44 `cacheLife` cannot be used at module scope. Calling it at the top level of a file will throw an error. 45 46 > **Good to know**: 47 > 48 > - Calling `cacheLife` is optional. If omitted, a default cache lifetime is applied. 49 > - Call `cacheLife` in the same function or component where caching is defined. Avoid abstracting it into shared utilities so the cache behavior remains explicit and easy to reason about. 50 > - If you call `cacheLife`, ensure only one call executes per function invocation. You can call it in different control flow branches, but only one should run per request. See the [conditional cache lifetimes](#conditional-cache-lifetimes) example. 51 52 ### Using preset profiles 53 54 Next.js provides preset cache profiles that cover common caching needs. Each profile balances three factors: 55 56 - How long users see cached content without checking for updates (client-side) 57 - How often fresh content is generated on the server 58 - When old content expires completely 59 60 Choose a profile based on how frequently your content changes: 61 62 - **`seconds`** - Real-time data (stock prices, live scores) 63 - **`minutes`** - Frequently updated (social feeds, news) 64 - **`hours`** - Multiple daily updates (product inventory, weather) 65 - **`days`** - Daily updates (blog posts, articles) 66 - **`weeks`** - Weekly updates (podcasts, newsletters) 67 - **`max`** - Rarely changes (legal pages, archived content) 68 69 Import `cacheLife` and pass a profile name: 70 71 ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" highlight={1,5} 72 'use cache' 73 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 74 75 export default async function BlogPage() { 76 cacheLife('days') // Blog content updated daily 77 78 const posts = await getBlogPosts() 79 return
{/* render posts */}
80 } 81 ``` 82 83 The profile name tells Next.js how to cache the entire function's output. If you don't call `cacheLife`, the `default` profile is used. See [preset cache profiles](#preset-cache-profiles) for timing details. 84 85 ## Reference 86 87 ### Cache profile properties 88 89 Cache profiles control caching behavior through three timing properties: 90 91 - **[`stale`](#stale)**: How long the client can use cached data without checking the server 92 - **[`revalidate`](#revalidate)**: After this time, the next request will trigger a background refresh 93 - **[`expire`](#expire)**: After this time with no requests, the next one waits for fresh content 94 95 #### `stale` 96 97 **Client-side:** How long the client can use cached data without checking the server. 98 99 During this time, the client-side router displays cached content immediately without any network request. After this period expires, the router must check with the server on the next navigation or request. This provides instant page loads from the client cache, but data may be outdated. 100 101 - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `stale` value (5 minutes, see [`staleTimes`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes)) 102 103 ```tsx 104 cacheLife({ stale: 300 }) // 5 minutes 105 ``` 106 107 #### `revalidate` 108 109 How often the server regenerates cached content in the background. 110 111 - When a request arrives after this period, the server: 112 1. Serves the cached version immediately (if available) 113 2. Regenerates content in the background 114 3. Updates the cache with fresh content 115 - Similar to [Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) 116 - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `revalidate` value (15 minutes) 117 118 ```tsx 119 cacheLife({ revalidate: 900 }) // 15 minutes 120 ``` 121 122 #### `expire` 123 124 Maximum time before the server must regenerate cached content. 125 126 - After this period with no traffic, the server regenerates content synchronously on the next request 127 - When you set both `revalidate` and `expire`, `expire` must be longer than `revalidate`. Next.js validates this and raises an error for invalid configurations. 128 - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `expire` value (never expires) 129 130 ```tsx 131 cacheLife({ expire: 3600 }) // 1 hour 132 ``` 133 134 ### Preset cache profiles 135 136 If you don't specify a profile, Next.js uses the `default` profile. We recommend explicitly setting a profile to make caching behavior clear. 137 138 | **Profile** | **Use Case** | `stale` | `revalidate` | `expire` | 139 | ----------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------ | -------- | 140 | `default` | Standard content | 5 minutes | 15 minutes | never | 141 | `seconds` | Real-time data | 30 seconds | 1 second | 1 minute | 142 | `minutes` | Frequently updated content | 5 minutes | 1 minute | 1 hour | 143 | `hours` | Content updated multiple times per day | 5 minutes | 1 hour | 1 day | 144 | `days` | Content updated daily | 5 minutes | 1 day | 1 week | 145 | `weeks` | Content updated weekly | 5 minutes | 1 week | 30 days | 146 | `max` | Stable content that rarely changes | 5 minutes | 30 days | 1 year | 147 148 ### Custom cache profiles 149 150 Define reusable cache profiles in your `next.config.ts` file: 151 152 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 153 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 154 155 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 156 cacheComponents: true, 157 cacheLife: { 158 biweekly: { 159 stale: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 160 revalidate: 60 * 60 * 24, // 1 day 161 expire: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 162 }, 163 }, 164 } 165 166 export default nextConfig 167 ``` 168 169 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 170 const nextConfig = { 171 cacheComponents: true, 172 cacheLife: { 173 biweekly: { 174 stale: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 175 revalidate: 60 * 60 * 24, // 1 day 176 expire: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 177 }, 178 }, 179 } 180 181 module.exports = nextConfig 182 ``` 183 184 The example above caches for 14 days, checks for updates daily, and expires the cache after 14 days. You can then reference this profile throughout your application by its name: 185 186 > **Good to know**: Any omitted properties in a custom profile inherit from the `default` profile. This also applies to inline profile objects passed directly to `cacheLife()`. 187 188 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={5} 189 'use cache' 190 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 191 192 export default async function Page() { 193 cacheLife('biweekly') 194 return
Page
195 } 196 ``` 197 198 ### Overriding the default cache profiles 199 200 While the default cache profiles provide a useful way to think about how fresh or stale any given part of cacheable output can be, you may prefer different named profiles to better align with your applications caching strategies. 201 202 You can override the default named cache profiles by creating a new configuration with the same name as the defaults. 203 204 The example below shows how to override the default `"days"` cache profile: 205 206 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 207 const nextConfig = { 208 cacheComponents: true, 209 cacheLife: { 210 // Override the 'days' profile 211 days: { 212 stale: 3600, // 1 hour 213 revalidate: 900, // 15 minutes 214 expire: 86400, // 1 day 215 }, 216 }, 217 } 218 219 export default nextConfig 220 ``` 221 222 ### Inline cache profiles 223 224 For one-off cases, pass a profile object directly to `cacheLife`: 225 226 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 227 'use cache' 228 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 229 230 export default async function Page() { 231 cacheLife({ 232 stale: 3600, 233 revalidate: 900, 234 expire: 86400, 235 }) 236 237 return
Page
238 } 239 ``` 240 241 Inline profiles apply only to the specific function or component. It should be used alongside the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive, and within the scope of the function or component. ## Usage ### Basic setup To use `cacheLife`, first enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file: ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { cacheComponents: true, } export default nextConfig ``` ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher const nextConfig = { cacheComponents: true, } export default nextConfig ``` `cacheLife` can only be used within a cache directive scope. Add a cache directive (for example, `use cache`) at the file level or at the top of an async function or component. `cacheLife` cannot be used at module scope. Calling it at the top level of a file will throw an error. > **Good to know**: > > - Calling `cacheLife` is optional. If omitted, a default cache lifetime is applied. > - Call `cacheLife` in the same function or component where caching is defined. Avoid abstracting it into shared utilities so the cache behavior remains explicit and easy to reason about. > - If you call `cacheLife`, ensure only one call executes per function invocation. You can call it in different control flow branches, but only one should run per request. See the [conditional cache lifetimes](#conditional-cache-lifetimes) example. ### Using preset profiles Next.js provides preset cache profiles that cover common caching needs. Each profile balances three factors: - How long users see cached content without checking for updates (client-side) - How often fresh content is generated on the server - When old content expires completely Choose a profile based on how frequently your content changes: - **`seconds`** - Real-time data (stock prices, live scores) - **`minutes`** - Frequently updated (social feeds, news) - **`hours`** - Multiple daily updates (product inventory, weather) - **`days`** - Daily updates (blog posts, articles) - **`weeks`** - Weekly updates (podcasts, newsletters) - **`max`** - Rarely changes (legal pages, archived content) Import `cacheLife` and pass a profile name: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" highlight={1,5} 'use cache' import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' export default async function BlogPage() { cacheLife('days') // Blog content updated daily const posts = await getBlogPosts() return
{/* render posts */}
} ``` The profile name tells Next.js how to cache the entire function's output. If you don't call `cacheLife`, the `default` profile is used. See [preset cache profiles](#preset-cache-profiles) for timing details. ## Reference ### Cache profile properties Cache profiles control caching behavior through three timing properties: - **[`stale`](#stale)**: How long the client can use cached data without checking the server - **[`revalidate`](#revalidate)**: After this time, the next request will trigger a background refresh - **[`expire`](#expire)**: After this time with no requests, the next one waits for fresh content #### `stale` **Client-side:** How long the client can use cached data without checking the server. During this time, the client-side router displays cached content immediately without any network request. After this period expires, the router must check with the server on the next navigation or request. This provides instant page loads from the client cache, but data may be outdated. - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `stale` value (5 minutes, see [`staleTimes`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes)) ```tsx cacheLife({ stale: 300 }) // 5 minutes ``` #### `revalidate` How often the server regenerates cached content in the background. - When a request arrives after this period, the server: 1. Serves the cached version immediately (if available) 2. Regenerates content in the background 3. Updates the cache with fresh content - Similar to [Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `revalidate` value (15 minutes) ```tsx cacheLife({ revalidate: 900 }) // 15 minutes ``` #### `expire` Maximum time before the server must regenerate cached content. - After this period with no traffic, the server regenerates content synchronously on the next request - When you set both `revalidate` and `expire`, `expire` must be longer than `revalidate`. content.text:
Done, and verified with a successful build — the route table confirms `/` now has a 1-hour revalidate (and 1-day expire, from the `hours` profile).

This Next.js version (16.3 canary) replaces the old `fetch`-options/route-segment caching with the **Cache Components** model, so per its docs I made these changes:

- **`app/page.tsx`** — converted `Home` to an async server component using the `'use cache'` directive, with:
  - `cacheLife('hours')` — the preset profile whose revalidate period is exactly 1 hour (the docs recommend presets over inline objects; `hours` is their designated "1 hour" profile).
  - `cacheTag('posts')` — so the entry can be invalidated on-demand via `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')` (background refresh) or `updateTag('posts')` (immediate, in Server Functions). Note `revalidateTag` takes a second "profile" argument in this version.
  - The page fetches via `getPosts()` from `lib/api` and renders the post list.
- **`next.config.ts`** — added `cacheComponents: true`, which is required for `cacheLife`/`cacheTag` to work. (Both are now stable exports from `next/cache` — no `unstable_` prefix.)
